summary:
MarsWalk is a robotic navigation and astronaut-guidance system designed to support safer exploration of the Martian surface. Combining real NASA HiRISE elevation data with an interactive 3D map of Phlegra Montes, MarsWalk enables users to select destinations and calculate terrain-aware routes using the A* pathfinding algorithm.

Our system analyzes terrain slope alongside experimental thermal and dust-cover indicators to estimate route difficulty, travel distance, and time. To bring this concept into the physical world, we developed a rover prototype using an ESP32, Arduino Uno, motor-control hardware, and an ultrasonic sensor for obstacle detection. A webcam and ArUco marker enable visual identification of the astronaut, supporting human-aware robotic navigation.

Developed with React, Three.js, Python, and FastAPI, MarsWalk connects planetary mapping, computer vision, and embedded systems. It explores how intelligent robotic companions could help astronauts navigate unfamiliar terrain while improving situational awareness during future Mars missions.
details:
MarsWalk: Intelligent Navigation and Astronaut Guidance on Mars

Overview

MarsWalk is a prototype planetary navigation and robotic guidance system designed to support astronauts exploring the Martian surface. The project combines authentic planetary datasets, interactive 3D terrain visualization, intelligent pathfinding, computer vision, and embedded robotics.

Our goal is to explore how scientific data and robotic assistance could improve route planning, situational awareness, and mobility during future human missions to Mars.

How MarsWalk Works

1. Interactive 3D Martian Terrain

MarsWalk uses a Digital Terrain Model (DTM) from NASA's High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) to reconstruct the Phlegra Montes region of Mars.

We developed an interactive 3D environment using React, TypeScript, Three.js, and React Three Fiber. Users can explore the Martian landscape, examine changes in elevation, switch between 2D and 3D views, and select destinations for route planning.

The terrain visualization preserves the geographic proportions and elevation measurements of the source dataset while using optimized rendering techniques to maintain interactive performance.

2. Intelligent Route Planning

When a destination is selected, the frontend sends its coordinates to a Python backend through FastAPI.

MarsWalk uses the A* pathfinding algorithm to search for traversable routes across a terrain-cost grid.

The routing model considers terrain slope, experimental thermal indicators, and dust-cover indicators to assign movement costs and avoid terrain exceeding the configured slope threshold.

After calculating a route, the system displays it on the 3D terrain and provides estimated distance, travel time, and a relative risk index.

These outputs are planning estimates generated by our experimental model rather than validated predictions of real mission conditions.

3. Thermal Emission and Surface Dust-Cover Analysis

To expand our analysis beyond terrain elevation, we used the USGS Astrogeology Mars Interactive Maps as a resource for exploring Martian thermal and dust-cover information.

Our project incorporates thermal imagery associated with the Mars Odyssey Thermal Emission Imaging System (THEMIS) and dust-cover information associated with the Mars Global Surveyor Thermal Emission Spectrometer (TES).

We prepared thermal and dust-cover image inputs for use in our experimental Python routing model. These inputs contribute relative environmental costs alongside slope.

MarsWalk also provides Thermal Emission and Surface Dust Cover Index visualization modes. Currently, the frontend uses illustrative color palettes derived from the terrain elevation rather than displaying calibrated thermal or dust measurements.

This distinction allows us to explore the integration of multiple planetary datasets while recognizing the scientific limitations of image-derived environmental indicators.

4. Physical Rover Prototype

MarsWalk extends beyond its digital navigation interface through a physical rover prototype.

Our team used an ESP32, Arduino Uno, motor-control components, a small robotic vehicle, and an ultrasonic sensor for nearby obstacle detection.

The Python backend converts calculated routes into sequences of scaled movement instructions, including turns, forward movement, motor parameters, and movement durations.

This provides a foundation for demonstrating how routes calculated from Martian terrain data can be translated into instructions suitable for a physical robotic platform.

5. Astronaut Identification Through Computer Vision

To incorporate astronaut awareness, our prototype uses a webcam and an ArUco marker.

The marker serves as a recognizable visual identifier that a computer vision system can detect, allowing the prototype to recognize the presence of a designated astronaut within the camera's field of view.

This approach demonstrates a potential mechanism for astronaut identification and provides a foundation for future astronaut-following and human-aware robotic navigation capabilities.

6. Human-Machine Interaction

MarsWalk combines its digital navigation dashboard with a human-machine interface (HMI) component in the physical prototype.

The navigation interface allows users to select destinations, view terrain information, request routes, and inspect calculated results.

Together, these components explore how human operators can interact with a robotic navigation system rather than relying on autonomous decision-making without user oversight.

Technologies, Hardware, and Resources

Frontend: React, TypeScript, JavaScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Vite, HTML, and CSS.

Backend: Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, and A* pathfinding.

Planetary data and resources:

  • NASA HiRISE Digital Terrain Model of Phlegra Montes.
  • NASA Mars Odyssey THEMIS thermal imagery.
  • NASA Mars Global Surveyor TES dust-cover information.
  • USGS Astrogeology Mars Interactive Maps for planetary mapping and data exploration.

Hardware: ESP32, Arduino Uno, ultrasonic sensor, webcam, motor-control components, and physical rover prototype.

Computer vision: ArUco marker-based astronaut identification.

Development tools: Visual Studio Code, Git, and GitHub.

Innovation and Creativity

MarsWalk integrates planetary science, software engineering, pathfinding, computer vision, and embedded electronics into a single astronaut-centered exploration concept.

Instead of displaying static maps, the project allows users to interact with real Martian topography, select destinations, calculate terrain-aware routes, and generate scaled robotic movement instructions.

By incorporating thermal and dust-cover information alongside elevation and slope, MarsWalk explores a multi-factor approach to route planning.

The physical rover and ArUco-based astronaut identification add a tangible human-robot interaction component, connecting the digital planning environment with a robotic demonstration.

Design Considerations and Challenges

Throughout development, our team considered several technical challenges:

  • Scientific data accuracy: Preserving the measurements and geographic characteristics of the HiRISE terrain dataset.
  • Rendering performance: Displaying a large, high-resolution Martian landscape interactively.
  • Terrain safety: Accounting for steep slopes and potentially difficult terrain during route calculations.
  • Environmental data limitations: Distinguishing image-derived thermal and dust indicators from calibrated measurements.
  • Physical implementation: Translating large-scale Martian routes into movement instructions for a small rover.
  • Astronaut awareness: Using visual markers to identify an astronaut within the camera's field of view.
  • System integration: Connecting the mapping interface, route-planning backend, and robotic demonstration.

Intended Impact

MarsWalk investigates how robotic companions and data-driven navigation systems could assist astronauts during future Mars exploration missions.

By combining real Martian elevation data with environmental information, pathfinding, and human-aware robotics, the project demonstrates an approach to evaluating routes and supporting navigation decisions before entering potentially difficult terrain.

Although MarsWalk is an experimental prototype rather than a flight-ready navigation system, it illustrates how publicly available planetary data and accessible robotics technologies can be combined to develop practical concepts for future human exploration.

Our long-term vision is a robotic companion that helps astronauts explore farther, navigate more confidently, and maintain greater awareness of their surroundings.
